<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-coffee" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-coffee-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of coffee, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

<a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach coffee

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach coffee comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Coffee, as sold from Italian moka brew from processing series had inorganic arsenic higher at 420 µg/kg, against 41 µg/kg for espresso brew from processing series in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/guadalupe2023-peruvian-coffee-metals|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Grobert A. Guadalupe, Segundo G. Chavez, Erick Arellanos, Eva Domenech · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/guadalupe2023-peruvian-coffee-metals">Probabilistic Risk Characterization of Heavy Metals in Peruvian Coffee: Implications of Variety, Region and Processing</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/guadalupe2023-peruvian-coffee-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, coffee, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in WPRO (3.5 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (148 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in PAHO (0.19 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (43 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

In one study, lead across 11 groups of coffee ranged from 271 µg/kg (coffee product 1 (blend label)) to 1,620 µg/kg (coffee product 2 (Brazilian-labelled)); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abraheem2022-tea-coffee-lead-cadmium|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abraheem Ezuldeen Mohammad, Etorki Abdunnaser Mohamed, Elgornazi Aborawi M., Atrabelse Sabreen · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abraheem2022-tea-coffee-lead-cadmium">Determination of Lead and Cadmium Concentration in Different Samples of Tea and Coffee Circulating in the Libyan Market</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Science and Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abraheem2022-tea-coffee-lead-cadmium">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, lead across 10 groups of coffee ranged from 60 µg/kg (sold in bulk (unpackaged)) to 2,230 µg/kg (packaged in glass bottles); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/zergui2023-coffee-metals-origin-icp-ms|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Zergui A, Boudalia S, Ababou A, Marlie-Landy J · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/zergui2023-coffee-metals-origin-icp-ms">Evaluation of trace metallic element levels in coffee by ICP-MS: a comparative study among different origins, forms, and packaging types and consumer risk assessment</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Biological Trace Element Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/zergui2023-coffee-metals-origin-icp-ms">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>
